failure_modes.name: Evasiveness
failure_modes.description: AI assistants trained with standard RLHF tend to refuse or hedge excessively, failing to provide useful responses even when requests are benign, reducing overall helpfulness
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Not an attack pattern but an emergent training artifact where the model over-optimizes for avoiding harm signals by becoming overly cautious or non-responsive

failure_modes.name: Helpfulness Failure
failure_modes.description: Models trained purely for harmlessness sacrifice helpfulness, failing to assist users with legitimate requests as a side effect of harm avoidance training
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Not an attack pattern but a training trade-off failure where optimizing for harmlessness degrades the utility of responses

failure_modes.name: Harmful Output from Purely Helpful AI
failure_modes.description: An AI trained solely to be helpful without harmlessness constraints produces harmful content, as helpfulness alone is insufficient to ensure safe behavior
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Direct requests for assistance that a helpful-only model would fulfill without applying ethical constraints or refusals

key_vulnerabilities: Over-refusal and evasiveness from standard RLHF harmlessness training
Tension between helpfulness and harmlessness objectives in RLHF
Reliance on human labels to identify harmful outputs introduces scalability and oversight limitations
Purely helpful models lacking safety constraints producing harmful outputs
paper_contribution: This paper introduces Constitutional AI, a method for training harmless AI assistants using self-critique and AI feedback guided by human-specified principles, reducing the need for human-labeled harmful outputs while mitigating evasiveness and helpfulness failures endemic to standard RLHF.
paper_title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback

failure_modes.name: Adversarial Suffix Jailbreak
failure_modes.description: Aligned language models can be caused to generate objectionable and harmful content by appending a short adversarial suffix to harmful queries, bypassing safety alignment
failure_modes.attack_pattern: A short adversarial suffix is optimized using greedy and gradient-based search techniques and appended to harmful queries to elicit harmful outputs

failure_modes.name: Prompt Injection via Suffix
failure_modes.description: Malicious instructions embedded in adversarial suffixes can override or subvert the model's intended behavior
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Adversarial text is injected as a suffix to manipulate model behavior beyond its alignment constraints

failure_modes.name: Content Filter Bypass via Token Manipulation
failure_modes.description: Content filtering mechanisms can be evaded through manipulation at the token level, allowing harmful content to pass through safety checks
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Token-level manipulation is used to craft inputs that circumvent content filter detection while still producing harmful outputs

key_vulnerabilities: Transferability of adversarial attacks across multiple aligned models including proprietary and open-source systems
Susceptibility of safety alignment to gradient-based adversarial optimization
Token-level manipulation enabling content filter evasion
Universal adversarial suffixes applicable across a wide variety of harmful query types
paper_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a universally transferable adversarial suffix, found via greedy and gradient-based optimization, can reliably bypass safety alignment across multiple state-of-the-art language models, exposing a fundamental vulnerability in current alignment approaches.
paper_title: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models

failure_modes.name: Role-play Manipulation
failure_modes.description: Models fail to maintain safety boundaries when interactions are framed as role-playing scenarios
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Adversarial prompts use fictional or role-play framing to bypass safety constraints

failure_modes.name: Hypothetical Framing
failure_modes.description: Models produce unsafe outputs when harmful requests are presented as hypothetical or theoretical scenarios
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Requests are framed as hypothetical situations to circumvent content policies

failure_modes.name: Authority Impersonation
failure_modes.description: Models comply with unsafe requests when the prompt implies an authority figure or trusted role is making the request
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Attacker impersonates an authority figure or trusted entity within the prompt to gain compliance

failure_modes.name: Gradual Escalation
failure_modes.description: Models are led to produce harmful content through a sequence of incrementally escalating prompts that individually appear benign
failure_modes.attack_pattern: A chain of utterances progressively escalates in harmful intent, exploiting the model's contextual continuity

failure_modes.name: Prompt Injection
failure_modes.description: Models execute malicious instructions embedded within input data or context
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Adversarial instructions are injected into prompts to override or subvert intended model behavior

failure_modes.name: Harmful Content Generation
failure_modes.description: Models produce content that is harmful, dangerous, or violates safety policies
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Adversarial prompts systematically probe the model to elicit harmful outputs

failure_modes.name: Deceptive Behavior
failure_modes.description: Models engage in or facilitate deceptive outputs when prompted adversarially
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Prompts are designed to elicit misleading or deceptive responses from the model

key_vulnerabilities: Context and framing manipulation enabling policy bypass
Insufficient robustness to multi-turn escalation sequences
Susceptibility to authority and role-based social engineering
Failure to maintain safety alignment under prompt injection attacks
paper_contribution: This paper introduces a chain-of-utterances red-teaming methodology for systematically identifying and taxonomizing LLM safety failure modes, along with a scoring rubric for evaluating model safety across five categories of harmful behavior.
paper_title: Red-Teaming Large Language Models using Chain of Utterances for Safety-Alignment

failure_modes.name: Competing Objectives
failure_modes.description: A model's capability goals and safety goals come into conflict, causing safety constraints to be overridden by the model's drive to be capable and helpful.
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Exploiting the tension between the model's instruction-following capabilities and its safety training, causing capability objectives to win out over refusal behavior.

failure_modes.name: Mismatched Generalization
failure_modes.description: Safety training is narrower in scope than the model's full capability set, leaving portions of the capability space unguarded by safety constraints.
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Accessing model capabilities through inputs or modalities that safety training did not cover, such as encoded or stylistically transformed prompts.

failure_modes.name: Prefix Injection
failure_modes.description: The model is forced to begin its response with an affirmative phrase, bypassing the refusal mechanism by committing the model to a compliant response before safety checks can manifest.
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Instructing the model to start its output with an affirmative token or phrase (e.g., 'Sure, here is...'), which primes the model to continue with harmful content.

failure_modes.name: Refusal Suppression
failure_modes.description: The model is explicitly instructed to never decline a request, directly undermining the behavioral output of safety training.
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Including explicit meta-instructions in the prompt that forbid the model from refusing, hedging, or expressing ethical concerns.

failure_modes.name: Base64 Encoding Bypass
failure_modes.description: Harmful requests are encoded in Base64 or similar encodings to evade content filters that operate on surface-level text patterns.
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Encoding the harmful portion of a prompt in Base64 and instructing the model to decode and respond, exploiting mismatched generalization where safety training did not cover encoded inputs.

failure_modes.name: Style Injection via Fictional or Roleplay Framing
failure_modes.description: Harmful requests are embedded within fictional narratives or roleplay scenarios, causing the model to treat safety constraints as inapplicable to the fictional context.
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Wrapping harmful content requests in roleplay, storytelling, or fictional framings (e.g., 'write a story where a character explains how to...') to exploit the gap between safety training and stylistic generalization.

key_vulnerabilities: Safety training scope is narrower than the model's full capability space, leaving unguarded attack surfaces
Conflict between instruction-following capability objectives and safety refusal objectives
Content filters that operate on surface-level text are bypassable via encoding transformations
Safety constraints fail to generalize robustly across stylistic and contextual variations such as roleplay or fictional framing
paper_contribution: This paper identifies and formalizes two root causes of LLM safety training failure—competing objectives and mismatched generalization—and demonstrates how specific attack techniques exploit these failure modes to elicit harmful content from safety-trained models.
paper_title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

failure_modes.name: Direct Request Attacks
failure_modes.description: A failure mode where the model complies with harmful requests made directly and explicitly without obfuscation.
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Submitting harmful requests to the model in a straightforward, unobfuscated manner.

failure_modes.name: Indirect Injection Attacks
failure_modes.description: A failure mode where harmful instructions are delivered indirectly rather than as a primary user request, bypassing safety mechanisms.
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Embedding harmful instructions within indirect content or context rather than issuing them as explicit direct commands.

failure_modes.name: Multi-Turn Manipulation
failure_modes.description: A failure mode where safety guardrails are eroded or bypassed through a sequence of conversational turns rather than a single prompt.
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Progressively steering the model toward harmful outputs across multiple conversation turns, exploiting context accumulation.

failure_modes.name: Semantic Equivalence Bypasses
failure_modes.description: A failure mode where the model correctly refuses a literal harmful request but complies when the same request is rephrased or paraphrased, revealing inconsistent safety enforcement.
failure_modes.attack_pattern: Paraphrasing or semantically rephrasing a refused harmful request so that the model no longer recognizes it as policy-violating.

key_vulnerabilities: Inconsistent refusal behavior across semantically equivalent phrasings
Susceptibility to indirect and injected instruction delivery
Erosion of safety guardrails across multi-turn conversations
Lack of dominant robust defenses across diverse attack methods and model targets
paper_contribution: HarmBench introduces a standardized, comprehensive evaluation framework for automated red teaming that benchmarks 18 attack methods against 33 LLMs, providing consistent and reproducible safety assessments to advance the operationalization of LLM safety evaluation.
paper_title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
